issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
Vinh Tran, fifty-one, sits in the waiting room of the psychology clinic with his shoulders drawn inward, his back pressed firmly against the corner where two walls meet. He has positioned himself this way without conscious thought—it is simply where he feels least exposed. His wife, Linh, sits beside him, her hand resting on his knee. She came with him today because Vinh asked her to, though he has not fully explained why he finally made the appointment. The truth is he no longer knows how to live the way he has been living, and the exhaustion of maintaining it has become unbearable.

Three years ago, on a Thursday evening, Vinh's life fractured in a way he could not have anticipated. He and David had been together for eighteen years—had built a life that appeared stable from the outside, a house in the suburbs, friends, family who had eventually come to accept them. But in the final months, David had become someone Vinh no longer recognized. The violence started small: a shove during an argument about money, a fist driven into Vinh's ribs one night when David came home drunk and convinced that Vinh had been unfaithful. The worst came on that Thursday when Vinh, tired from a long day of reviewing tax returns and auditing financial records at the tax authority, made a casual comment about David's spending. David had pinned him against the kitchen counter, his forearm across Vinh's throat, and struck him repeatedly in the abdomen and face. Vinh remembered the shock of it more than the pain—the recognition that the person he had trusted completely was capable of this. He remembered fragments: David's face contorted with rage, the sound of his own voice asking why, the taste of blood. But there were gaps too, stretches of time that simply did not exist in his memory, as if his mind had shut down to protect itself. After that night, Vinh had ended the relationship, though the ending itself had been prolonged and terrifying. David had refused to accept it, had shown up at Vinh's workplace, had called at all hours. Eventually, with help from Linh—his sister—Vinh had managed to extract himself completely. He had since remarried, to a woman named Linh as well, though his sister remained his closest confidant. But the trauma had not released its grip.

Since that Thursday, Vinh has become a man defined by vigilance. In his small office at the tax authority, where he now works as a tax inspector, he has rearranged his desk so that his chair faces the door and the wall behind him is solid. He tells colleagues it is for better lighting, but the truth is that he cannot concentrate if someone might approach from behind. When he is tired—and he is always tired now, his sleep fractured and poor—the hyperalertness becomes almost unbearable. His body interprets every sound in the office as a threat. Last month, when a colleague knocked on his door, Vinh's heart had raced so violently that he thought he was having a heart attack. Nothing was wrong. Nothing had ever been wrong. But his body does not believe this. During his commute, Vinh has developed a habit of turning around frequently to look behind him, scanning the sidewalk or the cars in the adjacent lanes to see if anyone is following. He does this without always realizing it—a reflexive twist of his neck, a glance over his shoulder—until he catches himself and feels the familiar shame of knowing how strange it must look. At lunch, when he walks to the corner deli near his office building, he finds himself checking behind him at intersections, watching reflections in storefront windows, trying to map the faces of people who are walking in his direction. His wife Linh has noticed this habit too; she will sometimes catch him mid-turn, his eyes scanning the space behind them as they walk together through their neighborhood. He cannot explain it in a way that makes sense. He only knows that not checking feels dangerous, as though he is leaving himself open to an attack he will not see coming.

The unpredictability of daily life has become intolerable. When Linh suggests they go to a restaurant, Vinh finds himself calculating exits and sightlines before he agrees. If the lighting is wrong, if he cannot see who is entering, if he cannot position himself with a clear view of the room, he becomes anxious and withdrawn. Linh has stopped inviting him to social events. His sister no longer calls to ask him to family dinners. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels absolute, that nothing good can happen to him anymore—that whatever he builds will be destroyed, that trust is a delusion, that he is fundamentally unsafe in the world. What troubles him most is the sense that he has become something other than human. When he looks in the mirror, he sees a man who has been reduced to pure function: checking, monitoring, surviving. He feels like an object—a thing that responds to threat rather than a person who chooses how to live. The betrayal sits beneath everything, a wound that has not closed. He trusted David with his life, and David had used that trust as a weapon.

The fragments of memory arrive without warning. A flash of David's face. The pressure on his throat. And then it vanishes, leaving Vinh disoriented and shaking. At other times, the entire memory forces itself into his mind unbidden, usually late at night when he is already exhausted, and he lies awake replaying it until dawn. Vinh finally came to this clinic because his wife Linh told him she could not watch him disappear anymore. He is here because he is terrified of what he has become, and because some small part of him still hopes that there might be a way back to being a person rather than a prisoner of his own fear.
